## Chapter 1

After the Typhoon’s worst, the shredded canvas was cut adrift, new reefs bent, and the Pequod once more took an East-south-east course—lo! a fair wind swinging astern, the yards squared to “Ho! the fair wind!—oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!” In obedience to standing order, Starbuck, reluctant and gloomy, went below to report the change. The cabin lamp swung fitfully; the thin, bolted door showed its fixed blinds; and against the forward bulkhead, the loaded muskets stood in their rack, shining.

An honest man, yet shaken by what he saw, Starbuck’s heart evolved an evil thought, so strangely blent with its good accompaniments he scarce knew it: “He would have shot me once—aye, there’s the very musket;—that one with the studded stock. Loaded? Aye; and powder in the pan; that’s not good. Best spill it?—wait. He dashes his heavenly quadrant; steers by dead reckoning through error; swears he will have no lightning-rods; vows he will not strike his spars to any gale. Shall this crazed old man be suffered to drag a whole ship’s company down to doom? If he were this instant—put aside—that crime would not be his. Is heaven a murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed? And would I be a murderer, then, if—” And slowly, stealthily, he set the musket’s end against the door. “On this level, Ahab’s hammock swings within; his head this way. A touch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again.—Oh Mary! Mary!—boy! boy! boy!”

From within, the tormented sleep gave tongue: “Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch thy heart at last!”

The yet levelled musket shook like a drunkard’s arm. Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; then, turning, he racked the death-tube again. “He’s too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go thou down, and wake him, and tell him. I must see to the deck here. Thou know’st what to say.”


## Chapter 2

Next morning the full light muffled the invisible sun; the sea ran like molten gold; the world boomed before the wind. Ahab, long silent, watched the rays ahead and astern; then, reined by some counter thought, hurried to the helm. “How heads she?”

“East-sou-east, sir.”

“Thou liest!”—and with his clenched fist he smote the steersman. “Heading East at this hour, and the sun astern?” Thrusting into the binnacle, one glimpse of the cards felled his uplifted arm: the two compasses pointed East, while the ship infallibly went West. “I have it! It has happened before. Last night’s thunder turned our compasses—that’s all.”

Accidents like this, in violent storms, have occurred: the heaven’s electricity and the mariner’s needle being of one essence, lightning will invert or annihilate the loadstone virtue; the needle never of itself recovers.

Deliberately Ahab took the sun’s bearing; satisfied the needles were exactly inverted, he shouted the new course; the yards were hard up, the ship once more thrusting her bows into the opposing wind. Whatever were his secret thoughts, Starbuck said nothing, issuing all orders quietly; the men murmured low; the pagan harpooneers alone remained unimpressed, or magnetized by Ahab.

“Thou poor, proud heaven-gazer!” said Ahab, eyeing the crushed quadrant. “Yesterday I wrecked thee, to-day the compasses would fain have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. A lance without a pole; a top-maul; the smallest sail-maker’s needle—quick!”

Facing the crew: “Men, the thunder turned old Ahab’s needles; but out of this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own, that will point as true as any.” With the maul he knocked off the lance’s head; bade Starbuck hold the iron rod upright; smote the rod, then the blunted needle; did some small strange motions; called for thread; slipped out the reversed binnacle needles; and horizontally suspended the sail-needle above the card. It quivered, vibrated, settled. Ahab stepped back, pointing: “Look ye, for yourselves, if Ahab be not lord of the level loadstone! The sun is East, and that compass swears it!” One after another they peered in and slunk away. In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph you saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.


## Chapter 3

Long had the Pequod neglected the log and line; rain had damped, sun and wind warped it; idle, it rotted under the bulwarks. Glancing on the reel, remembering his oath of the level log and line, Ahab cried, “Forward, there! Heave the log!”

The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzly Manxman came to the lee stern. The Manxman held the spindle high, the angular log hanging. As Ahab unwound a hand-coil, the old reelman ventured: “Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone—heat and wet have spoiled it.”

“’Twill hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet—have they spoiled thee? Thou seem’st to hold.”

The log was heaved; the coils ran, the reel whirled; the towing drag made the reelman stagger. “Hold hard!”—snap! the line sagged in one long festoon, the tugging log gone.

“I crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad sea parts the log-line. But Ahab can mend all. Haul in, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. Carpenter—another log; and mend thou the line.”

The Manxman muttered as they hauled the broken, dripping end: “Lines run whole and whirling out; come in broken and dragging slow.”

A crazed voice piped up. “Pip? whom call ye Pip? Ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high—looks cowardly—quickest known by that!”

“There can be no hearts above the snow-line,” cried Ahab, advancing. “Oh, ye frozen heavens! Here, boy; Ahab’s cabin shall be Pip’s home henceforth, while Ahab lives. Thou touchest my inmost centre, boy; thou art tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let’s down.”

The boy clutched his hand: “This seems to me, sir, as a man-rope; something that weak souls may hold by. Rivet these two hands together—the black with the white—for I will not let this go.”

“Oh, boy, nor will I thee, unless thereby I drag thee to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin.” And as they went, the Manxman eyed the rotten skein: “Best have a new line altogether. I’ll see Mr. Stubb about it.”


## Chapter 4

By Ahab’s levelled steel and his level log and line the Pequod held on toward the Equator—long passage, unfrequented waters, steady trades, monotonous mild waves—as of calm preluding riot. In the deep dark before dawn, gliding past rocky islets, a cry so plaintively wild and unearthly—like the wailings of Herod’s murdered Innocents—startled the watch. Christians shuddered “Mermaids”; the pagan harpooneers were unmoved; but the grey Manxman averred it was the voices of newly drowned men.

At grey dawn Flask recounted it to Ahab, hinting dark meanings. Ahab hollowly laughed: seals haunt those rocks; some dams and cubs, lost to each other, had kept company with the ship, sobbing with their human sort of wail. Yet the superstition clung; for in the very morning, a foremast-head man, perhaps not yet half waked from his sleep, fell—there was a cry, a rushing, a phantom in air—and then only a tossed heap of white bubbles in the blue.

The life-buoy—a long slender cask—sprang from its spring at the stern; but no hand rose to seize it, and the sun-shrunken staves slowly filled; iron-bound, the parched cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if to yield him his pillow. Thus the first Pequod man mounted the mast to look for the White Whale on his own peculiar ground—and was swallowed up. Some took it not as new foreshadowing, but as the fulfilment of last night’s presage; the old Manxman said nay.

A buoy must replace the lost: but no light cask could be found; hands were impatient for naught but the voyage’s crisis. Queequeg, by strange signs and innuendoes, hinted his coffin. “A life-buoy of a coffin!” cried Starbuck. “Rather queer,” said Stubb. “It will make a good enough one,” said Flask. “Bring it up,” said Starbuck, after a pause. “Rig it, carpenter;—the coffin, I mean. Dost thou hear me? Rig it.”

“And shall I nail down the lid, sir?”—“Aye.”—“And shall I caulk the seams, sir?”—“Aye.”—“And pay over the same with pitch, sir?”—“Away! what possesses thee to this? Make a life-buoy of the coffin, and no more.—Mr. Stubb, Mr. Flask, come forward with me.”

Left with his job, the carpenter grumbled of cobbling—legs one day, coffins the next, life-buoys out of coffins—yet set to it stoutly: nail, caulk, pitch, hang with a snap-spring over the stern; and, in a grim fancy, “thirty separate, Turk’s-headed life-lines,” that thirty lively fellows might fight for one coffin if the hull went down.


## Chapter 5

The coffin lay upon two line-tubs; the Carpenter caulked; oakum unwound in his bosom. Ahab came slowly from the gangway; Pip, like a shadow, behind.

“Back, lad; I will be with ye again presently.” Then, spying the work: “Life-buoy, sir. Mr. Starbuck’s orders,” said the Carpenter. “Beware the hatchway!”

“Thy coffin lies handy to the vault,” grimly answered Ahab. “Art not thou the leg-maker?—and the undertaker?—and now the bouy-maker? Arrant, all-grasping, monopolising, heathenish old scamp! Thou art as unprincipled as the gods, and as much a jack-of-all-trades.”

“I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do,” said the man; and, tapping, “the caulking mallet is full of music. Hark to it.”

“Aye; because the lid there’s a sounding-board—and what makes the sounding-board is this—there’s naught beneath,” said Ahab; “and yet, a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same.”

He turned aside, soliloquizing: “There’s a sight! There’s a sound! The greyheaded woodpecker tapping the hollow tree! Oh! how immaterial are all materials! A life-buoy of a coffin!—Does it go further? Can it be that in some spiritual sense the coffin is, after all, but an immortality-preserver!” Then, darkly recalling himself: “I go below; let me not see that thing here when I return again. Now, Pip; we’ll talk this over; I do suck most wondrous philosophies from thee!”


## Chapter 6

Next day a large ship, the Rachel, bore down, all her spars clustered with men. The Pequod was in brave way, but as the windward stranger shot nigh, her boastful sails fell like burst bladders, all life flying from the smitten hull. “Bad news,” muttered the Manxman.

“Hast seen the White Whale?” cried Ahab.

“Aye, yesterday. Have ye seen a whale-boat adrift?” came back, urgent and strange.

Ahab throttled his joy; answered no; and would have boarded when the stranger’s captain sprang to deck. Recognised for a Nantucketer, he told how, while three boats chased to windward, the white hump had loomed to leeward; the swift fourth boat was lowered, seemed to fasten, then—only a gleam of bubbling white water, and nothing more. Signals were set; darkness fell; far boats to windward first to be picked up; then stunsail on stunsail after the missing; try-pots kindled for a beacon; spare boats lowered; all night and day—no glimpse of the keel.

“Captain Ahab,” the stranger now besought, pale to the very buttons of his eyes, “for eight-and-forty hours let me charter your ship; I will gladly and roundly pay; only that—you must, oh, you must, and you shall do this thing. My boy, my own boy is among them.”

“He’s drowned with the rest on ’em,” muttered the Manx sailor; “ye heard their spirits.”

Ahab stood like an anvil, receiving every shock without quiver. “I will not go,” the other cried, “till you say aye. Do to me as you would have me do to you. For you too have a boy—though but a child and nestling safe at home—a child of your old age.”

“Avast—touch not a rope-yarn,” said Ahab. Then, prolongingly moulding every word: “Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I lose time. Good-bye, good-bye. God bless ye, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go. Mr. Starbuck, look at the binnacle watch, and in three minutes warn off all strangers: then brace forward again, and let the ship sail as before.”

The Rachel yawed hither and thither at every dark spot; her masts and yards thick with men; but still, by her halting, woeful way, she remained without comfort. She was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.


## Chapter 7

Ahab moved to go on deck; Pip caught his hand to follow. “Lad, I tell thee thou must not follow Ahab now. There is that in thee, poor lad, too curing to my malady. Like cures like; and for this hunt, my malady becomes my most desired health. Abide below here; they shall serve thee as if thou wert the captain. Aye, in my screwed chair; another screw to it, thou must be.”

“No, no! ye have not a whole body, sir; do ye but use poor me for your one lost leg; only tread upon me; I ask no more, so I remain a part of ye.”

“Oh! spite of million villains, this makes me a bigot in the fadeless fidelity of man!—and a black!—and crazy! Weep so, and I will murder thee! have a care—for Ahab too is mad. Hear my ivory foot upon the deck, and know I am there. Thy hand!—Met! True art thou, lad, as the circumference to its centre. God for ever bless thee; and if it come to that—God for ever save thee.” He went.

“Here he this instant stood; I stand in his air—and I’m alone,” whispered Pip. “He told me this screwed chair was mine. Here, then, I’ll seat me, in the ship’s full middle. Epaulets!—the epaulets all come crowding! Pass round the decanters. Monsieurs, have ye seen one Pip?—a little negro lad, hang-dog look, and cowardly!—Jumped from a whale-boat once. No?—then fill up again, captains, and let’s drink shame upon all cowards!—Hist! above there, I hear ivory—Oh, master! master! I am indeed down-hearted when you walk over me. But here I’ll stay, though this stern strikes rocks; and oysters come to join me.”


## Chapter 8

Now, with all other waters swept and his foe, as it seemed, chased into an ocean-fold; now, hard by the latitude and longitude of his wound; now, a ship had yesterday seen Moby Dick; and all late gammed ships concurred to show the demoniac indifference with which the White Whale tore hunters—now something lurked in Ahab’s eyes scarce sufferable for feeble souls. As the unsetting polar star through the livelong arctic night, so his purpose fixedly gleamed upon the crew’s midnight. Humor vanished: Stubb no more strove to raise a smile; Starbuck no more to check one. Ground to dust alike were joy and sorrow in the mortar of Ahab’s iron soul. Like machines they moved beneath his despot eye.

Yet, deeply scanned in confidences, Ahab’s own eyes seemed somehow awed by Fedallah’s; a gliding strangeness invested the Parsee; such ceaseless shudderings shook him the men doubted whether he were mortal substance or a tremulous shadow by some unseen being. Night nor day did any man certainly know him to sleep or go below. He stood for hours, never sat or leaned; his wondrous eyes said, We two watchmen never rest.

Nor might a mariner step the deck unless Ahab was before him—standing in his pivot-hole, exactly pacing between main and mizen, or fixed in the cabin-scuttle, his living foot advanced as if to step; his hat slouched heavily over his eyes; so that, however motionless he stood, day and night adding on, none could tell unerringly whether his eyes were closed or still intently scanning them. Night-wet clothes the next day’s sun dried upon him; he ate only breakfast and dinner in the open air; he never reaped his beard, which grew gnarled as roots of an overturned tree. Though some potent spell yoked him and Fedallah, they scarcely spoke; far parted in the starlight they gazed, as if each were the other’s forethrown shadow or abandoned substance.

Distrustful of others’ fidelity after long spoutless days, Ahab said, “I will have the first sight myself. Aye! Ahab must have the doubloon!” With his own hands he rigged a nest of basketed bowlines at the mainmast head; receiving the downward-reeved ends, he fixed one to his basket and prepared a pin for the other. Sweeping his glance from Daggoo, Queequeg, Tashtego (shunning Fedallah), he settled it on Starbuck: “Take the rope, sir—I give it into thy hands.” Arranged in the basket, he was hoisted; Starbuck secured the rope and stood near it; and so, with one hand clinging the royal mast, Ahab’s eyes commanded miles around.

Soon a red-billed sea-hawk wheeled screaming in a maze about his head; then shot aloft, spiralized downward, eddied again. “Your hat, your hat, sir!” cried the Sicilian from the mizen. But the sable wing was already before the old man’s eyes; the long hooked bill at his head; with a scream, the black hawk darted away with his prize. An eagle once flew thrice round Tarquin’s head, removing his cap to replace it—an omen good by the replacing. Ahab’s hat was never restored. The wild hawk flew on with it, far in advance of the prow; at last disappeared; and from the point of that disappearance, a minute black spot was dimly seen falling from that vast height into the sea.


## Chapter 9

The intense Pequod sailed on; another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, hove in sight, her shears bearing the shattered white ribs of a whale-boat. “Hast seen the White Whale?”—“Look!” the hollow-cheeked captain pointed to the wreck and to a rounded hammock the sailors were sewing. “Hast killed him?”—“The harpoon is not yet forged that ever will do that.” Snatching Perth’s iron, Ahab cried, “Here in this hand I hold his death! Tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning are these barbs; and I swear to temper them triply in that hot place behind the fin!” The other: “I bury but one of five stout men. Place the plank.” “Brace forward! Up helm!” flashed Ahab; and as the corpse splashed, a foreboding voice cried, “In vain, strangers, ye fly our sad burial; ye but turn us your taffrail to show us your coffin!”


## Chapter 10

It was a clear steel-blue day, air and sea hardly separable in that all-pervading azure; the gentle, woman-like air was pure and soft; the robust, man-like sea heaved with long, lingering swells. Aloft, white wings glided—gentle thoughts; below, leviathans rushed—murderous thinkings; yet those two seemed one. Like a royal czar the sun gave bride to groom at the tremulous horizon.

Tied up and twisted, gnarled with wrinkles, eyes glowing like coals in ashes, Ahab stood forth; and that glad air, that winsome sky, for a moment stroked him; the step-mother world threw affectionate arms about his stubborn neck. From beneath his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop.

Starbuck, careful not to touch or be noticed, drew near. Ahab turned. “Starbuck!”

“Sir.”

“Oh, Starbuck! it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild looking sky. On such a day—very much such a sweetness as this—I struck my first whale—a boy-harpooneer of eighteen! Forty—forty—forty years ago! Forty years of continual whaling! privation, peril, storm-time!—and out of those forty I have not spent three ashore. Oh, weariness! heaviness! Guinea-coast slavery of solitary command! Dry salted fare—fit emblem of the dry nourishment of my soul—while the poorest landsman breaks fresh bread! Away—whole oceans away—from that young girl-wife I wedded past fifty, and sailed the next day, leaving but one dent in my marriage pillow—wife? wife?—rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl. And then—the madness, frenzy, boiling blood, smoking brow—with which, for a thousand lowerings, old Ahab has chased his prey—more a demon than a man!—what a forty years’ fool—old fool—has Ahab been! Why this strife? how the richer or better is Ahab now? Behold. Brush this old hair aside; it blinds me, that I seem to weep. Locks so grey never grew but from out some ashes! Do I look very, very old, Starbuck? Close! stand close to me; let me look into a human eye; it is better than sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God. By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone!—I see my wife and my child in thine eye. No, no; stay on board—lower not when I do; when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be thine.”

“Oh, my Captain! noble soul! grand old heart! Away with me! let us fly these deadly waters!—home! Wife and child, too, are Starbuck’s; even as thine are the wife and child of thy longing, paternal old age! This instant let me alter the course! How cheerily would we bowl for Nantucket again!”

“They have such mild blue days in Nantucket,” murmured Ahab. “About this time—aye, it is his noon nap now—the boy vivaciously wakes; sits up; and his mother tells him of me—of cannibal old me—how I am abroad upon the deep, but will yet come back to dance him again.”

“’Tis my Mary!—She promised our boy should be carried each morning to the hill to catch the first glimpse of his father’s sail. Yes, yes! no more—it is done! we head for Nantucket! Come, my Captain, study out the course!”

But Ahab’s glance averted; like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil. “What nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what cozening hidden lord commands me; that against all natural lovings I so keep pushing—crowding—jamming myself
